title: Mysterious 10‑Minute X‑Ray Burst May Signal Dead Star Collision in Distant Galaxy
body:
A fleeting flash of high‑energy X‑rays lasting just ten minutes has been detected from a galaxy more than a billion light‑years away, and astronomers now think the brief burst may be the signature of a long‑theorised “kilonova”‑like collision between two dead stars. The event, spotted by NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and confirmed by ESA’s XMM‑Newton telescope, could provide the first direct evidence that merging neutron stars can produce ultra‑short, powerful X‑ray outbursts in addition to the better‑known gamma‑ray bursts and gravitational‑wave signals.

The burst was first flagged on 3 October when Swift’s Burst Alert Telescope recorded an abrupt rise in X‑ray flux from a region of the sky that corresponded to the outskirts of the spiral galaxy NGC 4993, a galaxy already famous for hosting the historic 2017 neutron‑star merger that produced both gravitational waves and a kilonova. Within seconds, the satellite’s X‑Ray Telescope began tracking the source, documenting a rapid climb to a peak luminosity of roughly 10^46 erg s⁻¹ before the signal faded below detection thresholds after about ten minutes. Follow‑up observations with XMM‑Newton and the Chandra X‑ray Observatory confirmed the transient’s position and duration, ruling out more common culprits such as flaring active galactic nuclei or tidal disruption events, which typically evolve over hours to days.

“The moment I saw the light curve, I knew we were looking at something unusual,” said Dr. Lena Martínez, an astrophysicist at the University of California, Santa Cruz, who led the analysis. “The rise and decay are far too steep for a standard accretion‑driven flare, and the energy released is comparable to what we expect from the merger of two neutron stars.” In a neutron‑star merger, the dense remnants spiral together, releasing a torrent of gravitational waves and ejecting neutron‑rich material that powers a kilonova. While most observed mergers have been identified through their gamma‑ray emission or gravitational‑wave signatures, this X‑ray‑only event suggests that some collisions may be “silent” in gamma rays but still unleash a brief, intense burst of X‑rays as the newly formed hyper‑massive object collapses into a black hole.

The discovery arrives at a pivotal moment for multi‑messenger astronomy. Since the first joint detection of gravitational waves and electromagnetic radiation in 2017, scientists have been eager to map the full spectrum of signals produced by compact‑object mergers. Theoretical models have long predicted that a short‑lived X‑ray flash could accompany the final plunge of the neutron stars, generated by the rapid formation of a relativistic jet that is either misaligned with Earth’s line of sight or quickly choked by surrounding debris. If the jet is sufficiently narrow or the surrounding ejecta dense, the high‑energy photons may be absorbed and re‑emitted as X‑rays, producing a burst that would be invisible to gamma‑ray detectors but detectable by sensitive X‑ray instruments.

Alternative explanations remain on the table, however. Some researchers propose that the signal could stem from a magnetar—a highly magnetised neutron star—undergoing a sudden magnetic reconnection event, or from a rare type of fast X‑ray transient associated with the collapse of a massive star in a low‑luminosity supernova. To discriminate among these scenarios, the team is combing through archival data for similar short‑duration X‑ray events and coordinating with ground‑based optical and radio facilities to search for any lingering afterglow that might betray the nature of the progenitor.

If the neutron‑star merger interpretation holds, the observation will expand the known phenomenology of these cataclysmic encounters and underscore the importance of continuous, wide‑field X‑ray monitoring. Future missions such as the Chinese Einstein Probe and the European Athena X‑ray observatory, with their enhanced sensitivity and rapid response capabilities, could capture many more of these fleeting flashes, building a statistical sample that will refine models of jet formation, ejecta composition, and the role of such mergers in forging heavy elements like gold and platinum. As astronomers tune their instruments to the high‑energy sky, this ten‑minute flash serves as a reminder that even the briefest bursts can illuminate the most profound cosmic processes.
